title: Diabetes and TB
dek: Hyperglycaemia blunts macrophage killing and raises poor-outcome risk. Screen both ways. PK and neuropathy monitoring get noisier; the regimen letters usually do not change by glucose alone.
story: Diabetes mellitus and TB associate bidirectionally: TB unmasks hyperglycaemia; diabetes increases risk of TB disease and of delayed culture conversion, relapse, and death. WHO recommends screening people with TB for diabetes and screening people with diabetes for TB in high-burden settings. This is not a different MTBC species.

Regimens remain WHO DS or DR algorithms. What changes is monitoring: INH/LZD neuropathy stacks with diabetic neuropathy; renal dosing for EMB/injectables if diabetic kidney disease; hepatotoxicity risk; and drug–drug noise with some oral hypoglycaemics and rifampin induction (sulfonylureas, others). Glycaemic control during therapy is part of the TB outcome, not an endocrine courtesy consult.
Cavities and atypical radiographs happen. Do not skip mWRD because the film “looks bacterial.” Prednisone for IRIS in a person with diabetes is a glucose bomb — plan it.
deep: A1c at TB diagnosis can be falsely shifted by illness; repeat after the intensive phase.
Rifampin induces metabolism of several diabetes drugs. Recheck glucose after week 1.
Obesity is not a reason to cap INH at half-dose without a PK reason; use weight bands honestly.
Diabetes is not an indication for adding a FQ to DS-TB “for severity.”

visual.caption: Hyperglycaemia as a host-defence covariate wrapping standard TB regimens. Screening is bidirectional; letters stay WHO.

check.prompt: Uncontrolled diabetes in DS-TB should usually:
choices: Keep WHO DS letters and intensify glucose plus neuropathy/renal monitoring
check.answer: Keep WHO DS letters and intensify glucose plus neuropathy/renal monitoring
check.why: No separate DM-TB regimen in WHO modules.

whyWrong.Stop rifampin forever: Induction is managed, not abandoned by default.
